Author: @tomoakhill8825
Content: This is utterly wrong. It depends on the FIRST looping. You want to tie a reef knot, (also called a square knot). This knot is formed by tying a left-handed overhand knot between two ends, and then a right-handed overhand knot via the same procedure, or vice versa. In Varitasium's words counterclockwise followed by clockwise. But clockwise followed by counterclockwise works just as well. So when Veritasium tells you to always make the second one clockwise, he is making the false assumption that everyone makes the first counterclockwise, with no reason to believe that is true.

Content:
I actually do it this way and never realized. I have, however realized that my shoes stay tied a really long time and my bow is parallel to the laces. 

To me it seems more natural. My right hand brings right side over left side then pinches both sides together, while my left hand throws the original right side around and through for the first knot. For the second, my right hand brings the right side to loop around my left thumb, then I pinch with my right hand while the left hand brings the original left side over and through.  For both parts, my right hand initiates then pinches, while the left completes the pull through. To me it feels awkward to do it differently.

Author: @993isgawd
Content:
I do a version of the bunny loop. Dunno if it has an actual name, but a coworker taught me this one years ago. Start with a simple overhand knot as usual, then take both ends of the shoelace and create each 'ear' of the bunny, just as you would normally do with the bunny loop technique. Cross the ears to create an 'x' with a 'hoop' now formed underneath it. But rather than just weaving one ear through the hoop underneath the 'x' and then synching it tight, instead loop _both_ ears, one in one direction over the right leg of the 'x' and then through the hoop, then the other in the opposite direction over the left leg of the 'x' and then through the hoop. Synch the resulting knot tight. Guaranteed that this resulting knot will NOT work itself loose, period. However I admit that it _sometimes_ can be a pain to untie, let alone tie to start with. Particularly with arthritic finger joints. 

Ask me how I know. 😣

Author: @vitriolicAmaranth
Content:
This is a silly way of presenting the information because the initial overhand knot or trefoil is chiral- Which means whether clockwise or counterclockwise gives you a square knot is, too. Furthermore, you didn't actually tie a shoelace knot (with loops), and from my experimentation, a traditional shoelace knot (making a loop then circling it and pulling a second loop through the circle, rather than just doing a second overhand knot with loose ends or with two loops) makes a knot that is about equally strong either way (though tying two loops in a second overhand does make a stronger knot as a square knot than the "standard" shoelace knot, and vice versa for the granny knot).

Perhaps the real takeaway is that "circling the loop" is a poor method to begin with. We should be teaching children to make two loops and use them to tie their first overhand knot but backwards. Voila, a better method of tying your shoes, and the instructions work as well for lefthanded people as righthanded people.

Author: @richardhowell7040
Content:
When I was about 30 years old, I noticed that the Bows formed by my shoelaces lay parallel to my foot, rather than perpendicular    
I decided to change how I tied them so that the boat would be perpendicular   what happened next I found to be very interesting and I’ve told the story many times
First, I would simply tie the initial half hitch that always starts a shoe tying    then I will proceed to make the bow    my reasoning was that I would examine how I tied that bow and simply do the opposite, and the bow would be perpendicular to the shoe) which is a square knot as you showed in your video)
So in other words, start with a half hitch go to make the bow , observe which direction I’m about to move to make the bow, but do the opposite so it comes out correctly. 

The surprise came a few days later when I realized that the urge to tie the bow clockwise and the urge to tie the bow counterclockwise had equalized.  
In other words, the fading urge to go counterclockwise, became equal to the growing urge to go clockwise    both felt natural forcing me to come up with a new algorithm

Content: Clockwise and counterclockwise depend on whether you tied the first phase of your knot with left over right or right over left. A better way to think about this is, if you tie first left over right (L/R), then your next move is right over left (R/L), and vice versa. R/L and again R/L, or L/R and again L/R will both get you a granny knot, with your bow loops oriented vertically. But L/R then R/L or vice versa, will give you the square knot with your bow loops oriented horizontally.

Author: @johnathansaegal3156
Content:
... and if you are left-handed, it's just the opposite. The right and left "loop" are reversed. When right-handed parents are teaching their left-handed children how to tie their shoe laces, this is where the first conflict of lefty vs righty begins.
It is where the kid realizes something about the world is wrong, but doesn't know why. It will be another fifteen to twenty years before that kid realizes the world has been built to oppose the left-handed person. Knots tied backward, doors open the wrong direction, can openers don't operate properly, wall-mounted pencil sharpeniers or anything with a cranks handle is "off", scissors, locks and latches, automobile controls... BOOKS, and writing on paper is all backwards to the left-handed person.
Things right-handed people take for granted are actually struggling points for left-handed kids to overcome and those kids don't even know they started life being at a disadvantage.
Maybe that's why most successful business people and politicians are left-handed... they had to struggle and overcome all through childhood and into adulthood. That tenacity to succeed at the little things worked its way into the larger issues of life.

Content:
I used to really struggle with tying my shoe laces due to undiagnosed dyspraxia as a kid. I wore velcro shoes until they stop selling them in my size and had to get teachers to tie my laces well into secondary school. Not only was I bad at tying them but they usually very quickly untied. I Got some Doc Martens at 16/17 and learned to lace and tie them in a military fashion, including this this technique, and was therefore forced to tie laces again. Author: @DijaFix
Content:
I don’t tie my shoelaces like either of those knots. I make a regular single knot and then I stretch both ends forward instead of to the sides, and wrap them around two fingers, pull them around the back, grab the nearest part of voth laces with those two fingers, and pull the cords through the first loop made around my fingers, making it a slip knot with two hanging loops and two hanging ends. It does not come loose on its own. It opens super easily when you intend to, you just pull on the end cords opposite the loops. It’s faster to tie than either of these ones too. And when you tie the knot you can pull the first single knot into the slip knot, tightening everything up nice and neat.

Pardon me if this explanation was unclear or I used wrong terms, English is not my second language and I’m not very well versed in knot terminology. I hope I got my point across tho?

Content:
Depends on your handedness too. I go counterclockwise, but my being a lefty means I naturally set it up in reverse as well. 

Better to think of it as over-under. Whichever side goes over on the first tie needs to go under on the second. When tying a bow it basically amounts to whichever side goes over on the first knot becomes the first loop that gets wrapped. To make it easier to remember, I tie the first knot opposite to what feels natural and then the rest of the tying process is the norm from there.

That’s how you get the beautiful bows on presents or belts with the ends both hanging down neatly from below.

Content:
I use the “Ian Knot”, learned about it when I was like 8 years old, fast and efficient easy to do. Make a loop with both ends and simultaneously pull them through each other to form an almost instant knot. 

Begin with a regular Left-over-Right Starting Knot

Make both ends into “loops” by simply doubling them back onto themselves.

Cross the loops and each hand uses the two fingers inside its own loop to grab the loose end of the other hand's loop.

Each hand releases its own loop and pulls the loose end of the opposite loop through its own.

There are plenty of visual aids for this online!

Author: @cardamom593
Content: Many of us were actually taught to do it counter clockwise. And that's for VERY good reason. The square knot on your shoes isn't strong enough to not come apart, due in great part to the shape of the string. Since the string is flat, but doesn't tie together flat, there's some wiggle room left over. When both loose strings are on the same side and something causes them to even slightly loosen, it causes a positive feedback loop of loosening. That causes both strings to come apart at once. However, using a granny knot, it is significantly less likely to come apart, since the likelihood of both loose strings being pulled on at once is lowered in comparison to the square knot. It still is easy to pull apart INTENTIONALLY, but that's because you can target the strings with the tip of your fingers, even though they're further apart and on different sides as compared with the square knot. In fact, that's intentional, because since, as i mentioned before, shoestrings are inherently a bit loose, they need to be able to be pulled apart in order to retie the knot, ideally, every time you put on the shoe. The granny knot strikes a good balance between lacking the likelihood to come apart on its own, while still being able to be pulled apart intentionally with relative ease.

_A simplistic analysis._

Tying the dual-slipped *Granny/Square* knot over a _doubled_ *Thumb* knot, will mitigate the problematic tendency of the *Granny* to capsize(*) rather than slip -- over the *Square* knot, which has the tendency to slip rather than capsize, which is the preferable condition.

Author: @bearslair2010
Content: I really like thhis Youtuber's channel, BUT his explanation is too simplistic as he's not discussing what you're doing prior to tying the loop.  His point is that you want to end-up with a square knot,  not a granny knot.  ONLY If at this time you're ending-up with a granny knot you can correct this by switching the loop direction.  So, what he's really trying to explain is that tying the loop needs to result in a square knot, But that also depends on the initial  part of tying the knot where you crossed the shoes strings, which can (like the loop) also be done two different ways.  So, if you presently tie a granny knot, but want to tie a square knot, either change the loop direction, OR change the initial crossing, But don't change both... or you'll still be tying a granny knot.

Author: @haldial2459
Content:
No, no, no! Every knot has two steps. If the first step is counterclockwise, the second must be clockwise to achieve a square knot. But if the first step is counterclockwise, the second must be clockwise to achieve the same result.

The square knot leaves the laces lying perpendicular to the shoe. The granny knot lies parallel to the shoe. When I was 8 years old, I realised why my laces were not nice and perpendicular and resolved thenceforth to tie them differently.

I could have changed either the first step of my usual knot or the second. I found it easier to change to a clockwise first step, leaving the final step as I was accustomed to. Still do the same seven decades later and have successfully avoided a lifetime of untidy shoe laces.

Author: @JesseBFournier
Content: I got a hypothesis for why we don't do it (I relearned to tie some years ago). There's a critical moment when we tie in the second part of the knot: it you're right handed and you tie clockwise, you'll realize you lift the thumb and in this moment your fingers pushing towards you: it easy to see, and you got four fingers to manipulate the laces. If you tie counterclockwise, you wont be able to lift your thumb in this critical moment and you'll have to do it with your index and "from the back". Bonus: If you tie clockwise the tightening phase at the end will be easier because counterclockwise forces you to cross you arms.

Content:
I learned this years ago. For about a week I looked like an idiot because I had to consciously think about how to tie the knot. 

It’s been years. My shoes almost never get untied. 

The kicker is what happens to the knots under pressure. If you pull on the laces (not the bow, act like tension coming from the eyelets on the shoe to pull on the knot) of a typically tied shoelace it will turn the bows vertical. This weakens the knot. 

If you reverse the loop to finish the shoe tying it no longer turns vertical and the knot is MUCH more secure.
